title: Market Failure Adventure 2: Public Goods & Asymmetric Info
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet public goods, free riders and asymmetric information.
meta_desc: Economics: public goods (non-rival, non-excludable), free rider problem and asymmetric information.
final_note: You explained the public good problem and three asymmetric information failures.

concepts.def: One side knows more than the other

walkthroughs.body_html:
A public good is both non-rival and non-excludable.

Examples: national defence, street lighting, clean air.

The market under-produces them because of the free rider problem — why pay when others will?

Solution: government provision financed by tax.

Rival but non-excludable: fisheries, atmosphere, aquifers.

Garrett Hardin (1968) 'Tragedy of the Commons': each user takes their share, overall stock collapses.

Elinor Ostrom (1990) showed communities can self-govern commons with clear rules — earning the 2009 Nobel Prize.

One party knows more than the other.

Adverse selection (Akerlof 1970, 'Market for Lemons'): used-car sellers know quality, buyers don't — good cars leave the market.

Moral hazard: insured drivers take more risk.

Principal-agent: managers may pursue own interest, not shareholders'.

mcqs.q: A non-rival, non-excludable good is a:
What is the difference between CPI and RPI as inflation measures?
options: CPI and RPI always give the same inflation figure.
CPI measures consumer prices and RPI measures retail prices — that's the only difference.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.

Both measure price changes via a basket of goods, but RPI includes housing costs (mortgage interest) and uses an arithmetic mean; CPI excludes housing costs and uses a geometric mean — CPI is the official UK target measure.

mcqs.q: What defines a pure public good?
options: Non-rivalry (one person's use doesn't reduce others') and non-excludability (you can't stop people benefiting) — e.g. national defence, street lighting.
A public good is anything provided by the government.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.
A public good is anything that's free.

mcqs.q: Why do economists generally argue against protectionism?
options: Protectionism always makes a country richer by keeping money at home.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.
A public good is anything that's free.

Tariffs and quotas raise prices for consumers, protect inefficient industries, invite retaliation, and reduce overall welfare — even when they save specific jobs, the cost per job saved typically exceeds the wage.
